claim: TGFβ is an important differentiation factor for cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) and alters the expression levels of several homing receptors during infection.
source: Transforming growth factor β (TGFβ) is an important differentiation factor for cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) and alters the expression levels of several of homing receptors during infection.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing TGFβ's effects on various homing receptors.

claim: SMAD4 is part of the canonical signaling network used by members of the transforming growth factor family.
source: SMAD4 is part of the canonical signaling network used by members of the transforming growth factor family.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge about SMAD signaling pathways.

claim: SMAD4 and TGFβRII are essential components of opposing signaling mechanisms that cooperatively regulate genes determining whether CTLs circulate or settle in peripheral tissues.
source: We show that these molecules are essential components of opposing signaling mechanisms, and cooperatively regulate a collection of genes that determine whether specialized populations of pathogen-specific CTLs circulate around the body, or settle in peripheral tissues.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the genetic experiments and phenotypic analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: TGFβ uses a canonical SMAD-dependent signaling pathway to downregulate Eomesodermin (EOMES), KLRG1, and CD62L.
source: TGFβ uses a canonical SMAD-dependent signaling pathway to downregulate Eomesodermin (EOMES), KLRG1, and CD62L, while CD103 is induced.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro and in vivo experimental data showing the effects of TGFβ on these markers.

claim: TGFβ induces CD103 expression via a canonical SMAD-dependent signaling pathway.
source: TGFβ uses a canonical SMAD-dependent signaling pathway to downregulate Eomesodermin (EOMES), KLRG1, and CD62L, while CD103 is induced.
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vitro experiments with TGFβ stimulation and analysis of CD103 expression.

claim: EOMES, KLRG1, CX3CR1, and CD62L are positively regulated via SMAD4.
source: Conversely, in vivo and in vitro data show that EOMES, KLRG1, CX3CR1, and CD62L are positively regulated via SMAD4, while CD103 and Hobit are downregulated.
evidence: This is supported by experiments comparing SMAD4-deficient and control CTLs both in vitro and in vivo.

claim: CD103 and Hobit are downregulated via SMAD4.
source: Conversely, in vivo and in vitro data show that EOMES, KLRG1, CX3CR1, and CD62L are positively regulated via SMAD4, while CD103 and Hobit are downregulated.
evidence: This is demonstrated through qPCR and flow cytometry analyses of SMAD4-deficient cells.

claim: Signaling via SMAD4 promotes formation of long-lived terminally differentiated CTLs that localize in the vasculature.
source: Intravascular staining also shows that signaling via SMAD4 promotes formation of long-lived terminally differentiated CTLs that localize in the vasculature.
evidence: This is supported by intravascular staining experiments showing the localization of SMAD4-dependent CTLs.

claim: CD62L (L-selectin) is an adhesion molecule that interacts with carbohydrates expressed on the surface of activated endothelial cells.
source: CD62L (L-selectin) is an adhesion molecule that interacts with carbohydrates expressed on the surface of activated endothelial cells (Steeber et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Naive CD8 T cells leave the bloodstream after CD62L initiates an adhesion cascade that results in transendothelial migration.
source: Naive CD8 T cells leave the bloodstream after CD62L initiates an adhesion cascade that results in transendothelial migration (Ding et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: IL-12 works with other inflammatory molecules to promote formation of short-lived effector T cells (TEFF) during the acute phase of infection.
source: During the acute phase of infection, interleukin (IL)-12 works with other inflammatory molecules to promote formation of short-lived effector T cells (TEFF) that are primed for rapid effector functions (Chowdhury et al., 2011; Cui et al., 2009; Keppler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Some pathogens elicit robust inflammatory responses and generate large populations of terminally differentiated TEFF cells that express KLRG1.
source: Some pathogens elicit robust inflammatory responses and generate large populations of terminally differentiated TEFF cells that express killer cell lectin-like receptor G1 (KLRG1) (Obar et al., 2011; Plumlee et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: KLRG1 is a membrane-bound adhesion molecule with an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motif in the cytoplasmic tail.
source: which is a membrane-bound adhesion molecule with an immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motif in the cytoplasmic tail (Ito et al., 2006; Rosshart et al., 2008; Tessmer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Stable KLRG1 expression identifies CTLs that do not convert to a conventional memory phenotype.
source: Although CTLs transiently express KLRG1 during antigen stimulation (Herndler-Brandstetter et al., 2018; Joshi et al., 2007), stable expression identifies CTLs that do not convert to a conventional memory phenotype (Dominguez et al., 2015; Plumlee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SMAD4 is an adaptor molecule that chaperones phosphorylated receptor-activated SMAD proteins (R-SMADs) into the nucleus to modulate gene expression.
source: SMAD4 is an adaptor molecule that chaperones phosphorylated receptor-activated SMAD proteins (R-SMADs) into the nucleus to modulate gene expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SMAD4 function.

claim: Loss of signaling via SMAD4 caused defects during formation of TEFF and TCM cells.
source: Extensive phenotypic changes indicated that loss of signaling via SMAD4 caused defects during formation of TEFF and TCM cells (Cao et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SMAD4 positively regulates EOMES expression and induces phenotypic changes that indicate progression toward a central memory phenotype.
source: We show that during transcriptional programming of newly activated CTLs, SMAD4 positively regulates EOMES expression and induces phenotypic changes that indicate progression toward a central memory phenotype, while formation of TRM cells is inhibited.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: SMAD4 inhibits formation of TRM cells.
source: We show that during transcriptional programming of newly activated CTLs, SMAD4 positively regulates EOMES expression and induces phenotypic changes that indicate progression toward a central memory phenotype, while formation of TRM cells is inhibited.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Very few SMAD4-deficient CTLs expressed KLRG1 or CD62L during IAV infection.
source: When we analyzed pathogen-specific CTLs during IAV infection, very few SMAD4-deficient CTLs expressed KLRG1 or CD62L, while abnormal CD103 expression was detected on CTLs in the spleen (Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Abnormal CD103 expression was detected on SMAD4-deficient CTLs in the spleen during IAV infection.
source: When we analyzed pathogen-specific CTLs during IAV infection, very few SMAD4-deficient CTLs expressed KLRG1 or CD62L, while abnormal CD103 expression was detected on CTLs in the spleen (Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: SMAD4-deficient CTLs proliferated and expressed IFNγ and TNFα at similar levels as wildtype CTLs.
source: We found that the mutation primarily influenced homing-receptor expression, since SMAD4-deficient CTLs proliferated and expressed IFNγ and TNFα at similar levels as wildtype CTLs (Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Neuraminidase activates TGFβ.
source: To elicit a mild inflammatory response in the lungs, mice were infected with IAV (X31-OVA) as neuraminidase activates TGFβ (Schultz-Cherry and Hinshaw, 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: KLRG1 is negatively regulated by TGFβ.
source: Prior studies show that KLRG1 is negatively regulated by TGFβ (Sanjabi et al., 2009; Schwartzkopff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Latent-TGFβ can be activated by viral neuraminidase.
source: Since latent-TGFβ can be activated by viral neuraminidase (Schultz-Cherry and Hinshaw, 1996), only small numbers of OTI-TR2Ctrl cells expressed KLRG1 after IAV infection, whereas most OTI-TR2KO cells expressed KLRG1 at high levels (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature and supported by experimental data.

claim: Only small numbers of OTI-TR2Ctrl cells expressed KLRG1 after IAV infection, whereas most OTI-TR2KO cells expressed KLRG1 at high levels.
source: Since latent-TGFβ can be activated by viral neuraminidase (Schultz-Cherry and Hinshaw, 1996), only small numbers of OTI-TR2Ctrl cells expressed KLRG1 after IAV infection, whereas most OTI-TR2KO cells expressed KLRG1 at high levels (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There was little difference between percentages of OTI-TR2Ctrl and OTI-TR2KO that expressed KLRG1 during the early stages of infection with LM-OVA.
source: In contrast, there was little difference between percentages OTI-TR2Ctrl and OTI-TR2KO that expressed KLRG1 during the early stages of infection with LM-OVA (Figure 1B), indicating minimal influence of TGFβ during bacterial infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There is minimal influence of TGFβ during bacterial infection with LM-OVA.
source: In contrast, there was little difference between percentages OTI-TR2Ctrl and OTI-TR2KO that expressed KLRG1 during the early stages of infection with LM-OVA (Figure 1B), indicating minimal influence of TGFβ during bacterial infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing similar KLRG1 expression in control and TGFβRII-deficient cells during LM infection.

claim: OTI-S4KO cells mostly lacked KLRG1 and CD62L expression after infection with both X31-OVA and LM-OVA pathogens.
source: The OTI-S4KO cells mostly lacked KLRG1 and CD62L expression after infection with both pathogens, indicating a defect during formation of TEFF and TCM cells (Cao et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: OTI-S4KO cells have a defect during formation of TEFF and TCM cells.
source: The OTI-S4KO cells mostly lacked KLRG1 and CD62L expression after infection with both pathogens, indicating a defect during formation of TEFF and TCM cells (Cao et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic data and supported by citations.

claim: OTI-S4KO and OTI-S4TR2-DKO cells expressed KLRG1 and CD62L at similar levels.
source: The OTI-S4KO and OTI-S4TR2-DKO cells expressed KLRG1 and CD62L at similar levels, whereas the increase in CD103 expression was slightly more pronounced on S4KO cells than OTI-S4TR2-DKO cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing the two cell types.

claim: The increase in CD103 expression was slightly more pronounced on S4KO cells than OTI-S4TR2-DKO cells.
source: The OTI-S4KO and OTI-S4TR2-DKO cells expressed KLRG1 and CD62L at similar levels, whereas the increase in CD103 expression was slightly more pronounced on S4KO cells than OTI-S4TR2-DKO cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing the two cell types.

claim: SMAD4 regulates activated CTLs via a TGFβ-independent pathway.
source: These data are consistent with other studies and show that SMAD4 regulates activated CTLs via a TGFβ-independent pathway (Igalouzene et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to other studies.

claim: OTI-S4TR2DKO and OTI-S4TR2Ctrl cells proliferated at similar rates.
source: The data show that OTI-S4TR2DKO and OTI-S4TR2Ctrl cells proliferated at similar rates, indicating normal T cell priming.
evidence: This is supported by CFSE dilution and BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: OTI-S4TR2DKO and OTI-S4TR2Ctrl cells show normal T cell priming.
source: The data show that OTI-S4TR2DKO and OTI-S4TR2Ctrl cells proliferated at similar rates, indicating normal T cell priming.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar proliferation rates observed.

claim: The majority of OTI-Ctrl cells in the lungs expressed KLRG1 and GFP (CX3CR1) at high levels and were primarily located inside the blood vessels.
source: The majority of OTI-Ctrl cells in the lungs expressed KLRG1 and GFP at high levels (overlaid histogram and bar graph) (Figure 1C) and were primarily located inside the blood vessels (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by intravascular staining data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: OTI-SKO cells expressed KLRG1 and GFP (CX3CR1) at intermediate/low levels, and some cells were located in the tissue.
source: Conversely, OTI-SKO cells expressed KLRG1 and GFP at intermediate/low levels (Figure 1C), and some cells were located in the tissue (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by intravascular staining data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: SMAD4 acts as a catalyst for terminal differentiation of CTLs.
source: Since small numbers of SMAD4-deficient CTLs expressed KLRG1 and CX3CR1 at high levels, the data indicate that SMAD4 acts as a catalyst for terminal differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SMAD4-deficient cells show reduced terminal differentiation markers.

claim: S4TR2-DKO mice experienced more severe disease than controls after IAV infection.
source: After IAV infection, S4KO mice experienced more severe disease than the controls (Hu et al., 2015). Since OTI-S4KO and OTI-S4TR2-DKO cells displayed similar phenotypes during infection, we used weight loss to measure of protective immunity. S4TR2-DKO and S4TR2-Ctrl mice were infected with X31-OVA and weight changes were recorded daily (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). As expected, the S4TR2-DKO mice lost more weight and recovered from infection more slowly than the controls.
evidence: This is supported by weight loss data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Protection against reinfection with IAV was not dependent on SMAD4 or TGFβ.
source: After 30 days, the immune mice (and uninfected controls) were challenged with different strain of IAV (WSN-OVAI) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). None of the immune mice experienced substantial weight loss after infection with WSN-OVAI, indicating that protection against reinfection was not dependent on SMAD4 or TGFβ.
evidence: This is supported by challenge experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: TGFβ and activins signal via R-SMAD2/3.
source: TGFβ and activins signal via R-SMAD2/3, while bone morphogenic proteins and related growth differentiation factors signal via R-SMAD1/5/8 (Fink et al., 2003; Takimoto et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Bone morphogenic proteins and related growth differentiation factors signal via R-SMAD1/5/8.
source: TGFβ and activins signal via R-SMAD2/3, while bone morphogenic proteins and related growth differentiation factors signal via R-SMAD1/5/8 (Fink et al., 2003; Takimoto et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: SMAD4 facilitates signaling by both TGFβ/activins and bone morphogenic proteins by chaperoning complexes of phosphorylated R-SMADs into the nucleus for gene regulation.
source: SMAD4 facilitates signaling by both groups of cytokines and chaperones complexes of phosphorylated R-SMADs into the nucleus for gene regulation (Massagué et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: When CTLs are stimulated with TGFβ, the receptor phosphorylates R-SMAD3 and induces CD103 expression.
source: When CTLs are stimulated with TGFβ, the receptor phosphorylates R-SMAD3 and induces CD103 expression (Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: After cancer cells were stimulated with TGFβ, R-SMAD2 and R-SMAD3 were phosphorylated and formed heterodimers that entered the nucleus in the absence of SMAD4.
source: Prior studies show some redundancy within the SMAD signaling network. After cancer cells were stimulated with TGFβ, R-SMAD2 and R-SMAD3 were phosphorylated and formed heterodimers that entered the nucleus in the absence of SMAD4 (Fink et al., 2003; Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Control CTLs did not express CD103 during culture with rIL-2, while this marker was induced during stimulation with TGFβ.
source: Consistently, the control CTLs did not express CD103 during culture with rIL-2 (plus and minus ALK5 inhibitor), while this marker was induced during stimulation with TGFβ (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The same pattern of CD103 expression was observed when CTLs lacked R-SMAD2 (S2KO) or R-SMAD3 (S3KO).
source: The same pattern of CD103 expression was observed when CTLs lacked R-SMAD2 (S2KO) or R-SMAD3 (S3KO).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: S23DKO and TR2KO cells both lacked CD103 expression under all conditions analyzed.
source: In contrast, S23DKO and TR2KO cells both lacked CD103 expression under all conditions analyzed, whereas S4KO, S4TR2KO, and S34KO cells expressed CD103 at intermediate levels.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: S4KO, S4TR2KO, and S34KO cells expressed CD103 at intermediate levels.
source: In contrast, S23DKO and TR2KO cells both lacked CD103 expression under all conditions analyzed, whereas S4KO, S4TR2KO, and S34KO cells expressed CD103 at intermediate levels.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SKI protein is a nuclear proto-oncogene that inhibits TGFβ signaling through interactions with SMAD proteins.
source: Sloan Kettering Institute (SKI) protein is a nuclear proto-oncogene that inhibits TGFβ signaling through interactions with SMAD proteins (Sun et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: SMAD4 interacts with SKI and creates heterodimers that repress Itgae expression (αE integrin/CD103) in CTLs.
source: A prior report found that SMAD4 interacts with SKI and creates heterodimers that repress Itgae expression (αE integrin/CD103) in CTLs (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: S4KO cells expressed CD103 at higher levels than S4Ctrl cells during stimulation with rIL-2.
source: Consistently, S4KO cells expressed CD103 at higher levels than S4Ctrl cells during stimulation with rIL-2.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro culture data.

claim: CD103 expression increased when S4KO cells were stimulated with TGFβ.
source: However, CD103 expression increased when S4KO cells were stimulated with TGFβ.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro culture data.

claim: CD103 expression did not change when S34KO and S4TR2-DKO cells were stimulated with TGFβ.
source: Conversely, CD103 expression did not change when S34KO and S4TR2-DKO cells were stimulated with TGFβ.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro culture data.

claim: R-SMAD2/3 are required for TGFβ to upregulate CD103 in the absence of SMAD4.
source: These data show that R-SMAD2/3 are required for TGFβ to upregulate CD103 in the absence of SMAD4.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that S34KO and S4TR2-DKO cells do not upregulate CD103 in response to TGFβ.

claim: When R-SMAD2 is absent, R-SMAD3 cooperates with SMAD4 to upregulate CD103 expression.
source: When R-SMAD2 is absent, R-SMAD3 cooperates with SMAD4 to upregulate CD103 expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing CD103 expression patterns in different mutant cells.

claim: R-SMAD2/3 entered the nucleus without SMAD4.
source: Imaging flow cytometry confirmed that R-SMAD2/3 entered the nucleus without SMAD4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by imaging flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: TGFβ inhibits TCM formation.
source: Since TGFβ inhibits TCM formation (Takai et al., 2013), we analyzed the cultured CTLs for CD62L (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Between 50% and 60% of the control CTLs reexpressed CD62L when cultured with rIL-2 alone, and the percentages increased to approximately 100% when the ALK5 inhibitor was used.
source: Between 50% and 60% of the control CTLs reexpressed CD62L when cultured with rIL-2 alone, and the percentages increased to approximately 100% when the ALK5 inhibitor was used.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Only 25% of control CTLs expressed CD62L when cultured with TGFβ.
source: Conversely, only 25% of control CTLs expressed CD62L when cultured with TGFβ.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 50% of S4KO, S34DKO, and S4TR2DKO cells expressed CD62L during culture with IL-2, but the numbers did not change when the ALK5 inhibitor, or exogenous TGFβ, was used.
source: Although 50% of S4KO, S34DKO, and S4TR2DKO cells expressed CD62L during culture with IL-2, the numbers did not change when the ALK5 inhibitor, or exogenous TGFβ, was used.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TR2KO and S23KO cells expressed CD62L at high levels under all conditions analyzed.
source: TR2KO and S23KO cells expressed CD62L at high levels under all conditions analyzed.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SMAD4 has dual functions during regulation of CD62L, since blocking TGFβ signaling was not sufficient to restore CD62L expression in the absence of SMAD4.
source: These data indicate that SMAD4 has dual functions during regulation of CD62L, since blocking TGFβ signaling was not sufficient to restore CD62L expression in the absence of SMAD4.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that SMAD4-deficient cells do not restore CD62L expression when TGFβ signaling is blocked.

claim: Between 50% and 90% of the control CTLs expressed KLRG1 at 8 dpi with LM-OVA and the percentages did not change in the absence of either R-SMAD2 (S2KO) or R-SMAD3 (S3KO).
source: Between 50% and 90% of the control CTLs expressed KLRG1 and the percentages did not change in the absence of either R-SMAD2 (S2KO) or R-SMAD3 (S3KO).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo infection data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Large percentages of CTLs expressed KLRG1 (80–90%) in the absence of R-SMAD2/3 (S23DKO), or a functional TGFβ receptor (TR2KO and ALK5KO).
source: Large percentages of CTLs expressed KLRG1 (80–90%) in the absence of R-SMAD2/3 (S23DKO), or a functional TGFβ receptor (TR2KO and ALK5KO), confirming that expression was repressed by TGFβ (Sanjabi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo infection data shown in Figure 2C and a citation.

claim: In the absence of SMAD4 (S4KO, S34DKO, and S4TR2DKO) only small percentages of CTLs expressed KLRG1, while the portion of CD103 expressing cells significantly increased.
source: Conversely in the absence of SMAD4 (S4KO, S34DKO, and S4TR2DKO) only small percentages of CTLs expressed KLRG1, while the portion of CD103 expressing cells significantly increased (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo infection data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: SMAD4 promotes formation of terminally differentiated TEFF cells via a mechanism that does not require TGFβ, or R-SMAD2/3.
source: Our data show that SMAD4 promotes formation of terminally differentiated TEFF cells via a mechanism that does not require TGFβ, or R-SMAD2/3.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that SMAD4-deficient cells have reduced TEFF formation even in the absence of TGFβ signaling.

claim: OTI-S4KO cells expressed EOMES (Eomes) and CD62L (Sell) at lower levels than the controls, while Itgae was upregulated.
source: We found that OTI-S4KO cells expressed EOMES (Eomes) and CD62L (Sell) at lower levels than the controls, while Itgae was upregulated (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Many signature genes that are associated with TRM cells in the small intestine were upregulated in OTI-S4KO cells.
source: Many signature genes that are associated with TRM cells in the small intestine were upregulated in OTI-S4KO cells.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The transcriptional profile of OTI-S4KO cells correlates with TRM cells isolated from the brain and liver, as well as CTLs that were stimulated with TGFβ in vitro.
source: We found similar correlations with TRM cells isolated from the brain and liver, as well as CTLs that were stimulated with TGFβ in vitro (Mackay et al., 2016; Milner et al., 2017; Nath et al., 2019; Wakim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3D and citations to published datasets.

claim: Early signaling via SMAD4 impedes differentiation toward a resident memory phenotype.
source: These correlations indicate that early signaling via SMAD4 impedes differentiation toward a resident memory phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the GSEA data showing that SMAD4-deficient cells have a transcriptional profile similar to TRM cells.

claim: S4KO cells produced more Itgae transcripts than S4Ctrl cells during culture with IL-2 and expression increased when TGFβ was added.
source: As expected, the S4KO cells produced more Itgae transcripts than S4Ctrl cells during culture with IL-2 and expression increased when TGFβ was added.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Hobit promotes formation of TRM cells.
source: Notably, homolog of Blimp1 (Hobit) promotes formation of TRM cells (Mackay et al., 2016; Parga-Vidal et al., 2021)
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: EOMES is expressed in TCM cells and downregulated by TGFβ as TRM cells settle in peripheral tissues.
source: and EOMES is expressed in TCM cells (Intlekofer et al., 2005) and downregulated by TGFβ as TRM cells settle in peripheral tissues (Mackay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: The numbers of Hobit transcripts in the S4Ctrl cells decreased when the ALK5 inhibitor was used, while expression in S4KO cells did not change.
source: The numbers of Hobit transcripts in the S4Ctrl cells decreased when the ALK5 inhibitor was used, while expression in S4KO cells did not change.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Hobit is induced by TGFβ and downregulated via SMAD4.
source: These data indicate that Hobit is induced by TGFβ and downregulated via SMAD4.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data showing differential Hobit expression in response to TGFβ and in SMAD4-deficient cells.

claim: OTI-S4KO cells produced fewer Klrg1 transcripts than OTI-S4Ctrl cells during the TEFF response at 8 dpi with LM-OVA.
source: The data show that OTI-S4KO cells produced fewer Klrg1 transcripts than OTI-S4Ctrl cells during the TEFF response.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: KLF2 plays a central role in transcriptional regulation of CD62L during the CTL response.
source: Krupple-like factor 2 (KLF2) plays a central role in transcriptional regulation of CD62L during the CTL response (Takada et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: S4KO cells produced fewer Sell transcripts than S4Ctrl cells during culture with rIL-2.
source: S4KO cells produced fewer Sell transcripts than S4Ctrl cells during culture with rIL-2.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The numbers of Sell transcripts in S4Ctrl cells decreased during stimulation with TGFβ, while expression in S4KO cells did not change.
source: The numbers of Sell transcripts in S4Ctrl cells decreased during stimulation TGFβ, while expression in S4KO cells did not change.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: CD62L is induced via SMAD4, and downregulated by TGFβ.
source: These data indicate that CD62L is induced via SMAD4, and downregulated by TGFβ.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data showing differential Sell expression in response to TGFβ and in SMAD4-deficient cells.

claim: The numbers of Klf2 transcripts were not modified by SMAD4 or TGFβ.
source: The numbers of Klf2 transcripts were not modified by SMAD4 or TGFβ.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data.

claim: OTI-S4KO cells produce fewer Eomes transcripts than OTI-S4Ctrl cells during IAV infection.
source: Our sequencing data show that OTI-S4KO cells produce fewer Eomes transcripts than OTI-S4Ctrl cells during IAV infection (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The numbers of Eomes transcripts in S4Ctrl cells transiently decreased during culture with rIL-2 (72 hr after TcR stimulation) and returned to baseline at 96 hr.
source: The numbers of Eomes transcripts in S4Ctrl cells transiently decreased during culture with rIL-2 (72 hr after TcR stimulation) and returned to baseline at 96 hr.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Eomes was downregulated by TGFβ at 72 and 96 hr after TcR stimulation.
source: Eomes was downregulated by TGFβ at both time points.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: S4KO cells produced very few Eomes transcripts compared to S4Ctrl cells during culture with IL-2 and did not respond to TGFβ.
source: Importantly, S4KO cells produced very few Eomes transcripts that S4Ctrl cells during culture with IL-2 and did not respond to TGFβ.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: EOMES was induced via SMAD4 and downregulated by TGFβ.
source: These data confirmed that EOMES was induced via SMAD4 and downregulated by TGFβ.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data showing differential Eomes expression in response to TGFβ and in SMAD4-deficient cells.

claim: OTI-TR2KO cells expressed EOMES at higher levels than OTI-TR2Ctrl cells at all time points analyzed during LM-OVA infection.
source: OTI-TR2KO cells expressed EOMES at higher levels than OTI-TR2Ctrl cells at all time point analyzed (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: OTI-S4KO cells expressed EOMES at lower levels than OTI-S4Ctrl cells during LM-OVA infection.
source: whereas OTI-S4KO cells expressed EOMES at lower levels than OTI-S4Ctrl cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by intracellular staining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: EOMES was concentrated in the nuclei of exhausted CTLs after LCMV infection.
source: When CTLs were analyzed after LCMV infection, imaging flow cytometry showed that EOMES was concentrated in the nuclei of exhausted CTLs (McLane et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: OTI-S4KO cells expressed EOMES at lower levels than OTI-S4Ctrl at 8 dpi with LM-OVA, and a smaller percentage of the protein was located in the nuclei.
source: The OTI-S4KO cells expressed EOMES at lower levels than OTI-S4Ctrl, and a smaller percentage of the protein was located in the nuclei where it could influence gene expression (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: KLRG1+ CTLs from TR2KO and TR2Ctrl mice show similar patterns of EOMES expression.
source: KLRG1+ CTLs from TR2KO and TR2Ctrl mice show similar patterns of EOMES expression.
evidence: This is supported by imaging flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: TR2KO cells expressed EOMES at higher levels than the controls when gating on KLRG1-negative cells.
source: Gating on KLRG1-negative cells showed that TR2KO cells expressed EOMES at higher levels than the controls (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by imaging flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: EOMES expression in KLRG1+ CTLs was not altered by TGFβ.
source: EOMES expression in KLRG1+ CTLs was not altered by TGFb.
evidence: This is supported by imaging flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The promoter region for the Eomes gene includes multiple SMAD4-binding sites.
source: The data show that the promoter region for the Eomes gene includes multiple SMAD4-binding sites.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: EOMES must be downregulated before TRM cells express CD103.
source: Prior studies indicate that EOMES must be downregulated before TRM cells express CD103 (Mackay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Reduced EOMES and T-bet expression facilitated TRM development.
source: Consistently, others found that reduced EOMES and T-bet expression facilitated TRM development (Laidlaw et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: When EOMES was expressed ectopically, smaller percentages of S4KO and S4Ctrl cells expressed CD103, while the percentages of CD62L+ CTLs increased.
source: When EOMES was expressed ectopically, smaller percentages of S4KO and S4Ctrl cells expressed CD103, while the percentages of CD62L+ CTLs increased (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by retroviral transduction experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: GFP+ cells in lungs expressed CD103 at reduced levels after transduction with the EOMES-IRES-GFP vector.
source: GFP+ cells in lungs expressed CD103 at reduced levels after transduction with the EOMES-IRES-GFP vector (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo transduction experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Ectopic EOMES expression partially restored the phenotype of S4KO cells, and induced a shift toward a central memory phenotype.
source: These experiments show that ectopic EOMES expression partially restored the phenotype of S4KO cells, and induced a shift toward a central memory phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the retroviral transduction experiments showing changes in CD103 and CD62L expression.

claim: Ectopic SMAD4 expression induced a shift toward a TCM phenotype in S4KO cells.
source: We also used the (MSCV)-IRES-GFP (pMIG) vector to express SMAD4 ectopically and also observed a shift toward a TCM phenotype in S4KO cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by retroviral transduction experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Naive CD8 T cells are not a uniform cell population.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate that naive CD8 T cells are not a uniform cell population.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Naive CD8 T cells give rise to mixed populations of TEFF and memory CD8 T cells.
source: Early studies used limiting-dilution assays and fate-mapping experiments to show that naive CD8 T cells give rise to mixed populations of TEFF and memory CD8 T cells (Plumlee et al., 2015; Stemberger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: TEFF and memory CD8 T cells are products of asymmetric cell division.
source: Others found unequal inheritance of genetic markers during TEFF formation, indicating that TEFF and memory CD8 T cells are products of asymmetric cell division (Chang et al., 2011; Pollizzi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: The differentiation program for memory CD8 T cells begins soon after antigen stimulation, as the IL-7 receptor (CD127) is expressed on CTLs that are predisposed toward memory formation and absent from TEFF cells that express KLRG1.
source: Other studies indicate that the differentiation program for memory CD8 T cells begins soon after antigen stimulation, as the IL-7 receptor (CD127) is expressed CTLs that are predisposed toward memory formation and absent from TEFF cells that express KLRG1 (Kaech et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Transcriptome analysis revealed the presence of TRM precursors in a pool of circulating TEFF cells.
source: Transcriptome analysis also revealed the presence of TRM precursors in a pool of circulating TEFF cells (Kok et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Migratory DCs that activate TGFβ can precondition naive CD8 T cells to become TRM cells that localize in peripheral tissues.
source: Other data indicate that programming occurs at an early stage of diffrentiation, since migratory DCs that activate TGFβ can precondition naive CD8 T cells to become TRM cells that localize in peripheral tissues (Mani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: The population dynamics of clonal populations of antigen-specific CD8 T cells reflected the inflammatory environment that developed during infection.
source: The study showed that the population dynamics reflected the inflammatory environment that developed during infection (Plumlee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Large numbers of TEFF cells expressed KLRG1 during infection with LM, while this marker was less prevalent during infection with Vesicular Stomatitis Virus.
source: Large numbers of TEFF cells expressed KLRG1 during infection with LM, while this marker was less prevalent during infection with Vesicular Stomatitis Virus.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: IL-12 supports TEFF formation.
source: Several cytokines are known to influence the 'fate decisions' of newly activated CTLs, including IL-12 which supports TEFF formation (Mescher et al., 2006)
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: TGFβ has anti-inflammatory properties and encourages TRM cells to settle in peripheral tissues.
source: whereas TGFβ has anti-inflammatory properties and encourages TRM cells to settle in peripheral tissues (Skon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Signaling via SMAD4 is required for formation of TEFF and TCM cells.
source: Several studies show that signaling via SMAD4 is required for formation of TEFF and TCM cells, whereas TGFβ creates a bias toward TRM development (Cao et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2015; Mackay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: TGFβ creates a bias toward TRM development.
source: Several studies show that signaling via SMAD4 is required for formation of TEFF and TCM cells, whereas TGFβ creates a bias toward TRM development (Cao et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2015; Mackay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: SMAD4 and TGFβ control a key bifurcation in the differentiation pathway of antiviral CTLs, by regulating the same genes in opposite directions.
source: Importantly, these opposing pathways control a key bifurcation in the differentiation pathway of antiviral CTLs, by regulating the same genes in opposite directions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cell-state impacts susceptibility to TGFβ.
source: There is evidence that cell-state impacts susceptibility to TGFβ, since we previously found that TCM cells did not upregulate CD103 during stimulation with TGFβ (Suarez-Ramirez et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: TCM cells did not upregulate CD103 during stimulation with TGFβ.
source: There is evidence that cell-state impacts susceptibility to TGFβ, since we previously found that TCM cells did not upregulate CD103 during stimulation with TGFβ (Suarez-Ramirez et al., 2019)
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature by the authors.

claim: KLRG1+ CTLs maintain EOMES expression in the presence of TGFβ.
source: and our current study shows that KLRG1+ CTLs maintain EOMES expression in the presence of TGFβ (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by imaging flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: SMAD proteins modulate gene expression through interactions with numerous transcription factors, including the protooncogene SKI.
source: SMAD proteins modulate gene expression through interactions with numerous transcription factors, including the protooncogene SKI and forms heterodimers that repress the Itgae gene (CD103) (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: CD103 is downregulated via SMAD4-dependent induction of EOMES.
source: Our data show that CD103 is also downregulated via SMAD4-dependent induction of EOMES.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Reduced numbers of TRM cells were found in the skin of HSV infected mice when EOMES and T-bet were expressed at high levels using retroviral vectors.
source: Others used retroviral vectors to ectopically express T-box transcription factors in activated CTLs and found reduced numbers of TRM cells in the skin of HSV infected mice when EOMES and T-bet were expressed at high levels (Mackay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Zeb1 and Zeb2 are homologous proteins that serve opposing functions during memory formation and are inversely regulated by TGFβ.
source: The major players include Zeb1 and Zeb2, which are homologous proteins that serve opposing functions during memory formation and are inversely regulated by TGFβ.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: Zeb1 expression increases in maturing memory CD8+ T cells during exposure to TGFβ, whereas Zeb2 is downregulated.
source: Zeb1 expression increases in maturing memory CD8+ T cells during exposure to TGFβ, whereas Zeb2 is downregulated (Dominguez et al., 2015; Guan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: DNA-binding inhibitors Id2 and Id3 have reciprocal functions during fate determination of activated CTLs.
source: Other studies indicate that DNA-binding inhibitors Id2 and Id3 also have reciprocal functions during fate determination of activated CTLs (Ji et al., 2011; Omilusik et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.
